summary.text: A 95-year-old woman with Alzheimer’s disease residing in a nursing facility had fallen three weeks earlier and sustained a right femoral fracture, had surgery at another hospital and returned for rehabilitation. Gross hematuria was noted two days before admission without any change in consciousness. On the day of admission she did not respond and was found to have impaired consciousness, and was brought to the hospital by ambulance.

On arrival GCS was E1V2M4 with heart rate 105 and no other abnormal examination findings. Blood tests showed ammonia 168 micrograms per deciliter, leukocytosis, renal dysfunction and normal liver function tests. Catheterized urine was turbid and purulent with gross hematuria and alkaline on urinalysis, and ultrasonography showed urine with echogenic debris retained in the bladder, and no hydronephrosis; head CT showed no abnormal findings.

After bladder catheterization and about 1,000 milliliters of intravenous fluids her consciousness improved to GCS E1V3M5, so cerebrospinal fluid examination and brain MRI were not done. Ceftazidime was started for a presumed urinary tract infection. By the next morning GCS was E3V5M6 and ammonia had normalized to 35 micrograms per deciliter. Urine culture grew Corynebacterium urealyticum several days later.

Neurogenic bladder was diagnosed when spontaneous urination did not occur after the catheter was once removed, and the catheter was reinserted. Vancomycin was considered but no additional antimicrobial therapy was given and ceftazidime was discontinued. She was discharged back to the nursing facility on hospital day 12 with the urethral balloon catheter left in place.

article_limitations: The article has no figures and no supplements; no visual review applies.
Table 2 summarises 33 literature-review cases; only the row labelled "This case" is attributed to the index patient, the other 32 rows and the review percentages are cohort data.
Table 2 case number and reference number cells for the patient row are bibliographic identifiers and not recorded as clinical facts.
Urine pH differs between the text (8.0) and the Table 2 patient row (8.5); both are quarantined.
Table 2 time to improvement in consciousness (2 days) differs from the text describing improvement within the hour after catheter insertion; both are quarantined.
Fracture type (femoral neck vs trochanteric) and residence (nursing facility vs home) differ between the case description and the discussion; both versions are quarantined.
Table 1 arrows are recorded as high/low flags only as printed; unmarked cells have no flag, and no flags come from reference ranges.
Author speculation about mechanism (residual urine infected, ammonia absorption via the bladder wall) is not recorded as patient fact.

Several events (culture result, catheter removal and reinsertion, ceftazidime start) have no stated time relative to the day of admission; they are left unordered rather than ordered by paragraph position.
